newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed slams NATO as Russian critics sharpen knives.
newsitem.headline: Lebed slams NATO as Russian critics sharpen knives.

text.p: Russian security tsar Alexander Lebed fired a new broadside against NATO's eastward expansion plans on Thursday, a day after ending a visit to the alliance's headquarters which won praise from its leaders.

The outspoken reserve general, lauded in Brussels as "a man with whom you could negotiate", returned to Russia to find his critics sharpening their knives over what they portrayed as a failure to win any concessions from NATO.

Lebed, crowned Russia's most trusted politician by a new opinion poll, responded by accusing his rivals of missing golden opportunities to improve ties with NATO and then reverted to the tough talk that usually goes down well in Moscow.
"Will NATO's eastward expansion, towards our borders, towards the Baltic republics boost Russia's security?" Itar-Tass quoted him as telling a scientific conference.
"Nobody can guarantee that it won't occur to someone at some time to do to us what was recently done to Iraq."
Lebed, 46, was referring to U.S. missile attacks on Iraq.

His renewed criticism of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation is unlikely to shock alliance officials, some of whom realise the political risks of praising NATO to a Russian public brought up on a diet of criticism.
Moscow has long depicted NATO's plans to take in countries of central and eastern Europe as a threat to its security.

Praise from NATO, Moscow's former Cold War foe, is ammunition for Lebed's rivals in a battle for influence as President Boris Yeltsin remains out of the Kremlin awaiting heart surgery. The operation is expected in about two months.
While Lebed was in Brussels, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov continued the offensive against Lebed by publicly criticising one of his aides.

The opposition-dominated lower house of parliament, which has already blasted Lebed over a controversial peace deal which he signed to end fighting in rebel Chechnya, summoned Lebed to clarify his position on NATO later this month.
A spokesman for the Security Council, the small group of leaders of which Lebed is the secretary, said Lebed was satisfied with his trip to Brussels and would report to Yeltsin.

But in comments suggesting Lebed may seek a large say in or even control of Russia's NATO policy, the spokesman said: "Lebed thinks the last year has been a year of squandered opportunities in cooperation between Russia and NATO."

The spokesman also played down the significance of Lebed's suggestion in Brussels that Moscow's big threat was from the south, saying: "This does not mean that Russia has once and for all reconciled itself to NATO's eastward expansion."

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was quoted as repeating his opposition to NATO enlargement, saying it risked creating new lines of division. However, he added, Russia may have to accept the alliance may expand in spite of its objections.
If that happened, Interfax news agency quoted him saying, Moscow would pursue a special relationship with NATO, including some form of participation in its "military infrastructure".
Publication of a new opinion poll in the liberal Sevodnya newspaper offered some respite for Lebed.
Forty percent of people polled told the VTsIOM agency that Lebed was the Russian politician they respected most.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov was second with 16 percent, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin polled 14 percent. Yeltsin, re-elected on July 3 but now in a sanatorium awaiting heart surgery, was fifth on 11 percent. The poll of 2,430 people was carried out between September 6 and 29.
